title: LatticeSMC: Where to Spend Inference-TimeCompute in Chunked Sequence Generators

paper.title: LatticeSMC: Where to Spend Inference-Time Compute in Chunked Sequence Generators
paper.abstract: Abstract Long-form generators for music, motion and video produce a sequence chunk by chunk, each chunk by iterative denoising, while the rewards that matter are defined on the whole sequence. Existing inference-time steering methods act on one axis of this process at a time, best-of-N at the end, Feynman-Kac steering across denoising steps, streaming pipelines across chunks, and have been compared under different return rules at unmatched compute. We introduce budget-matched chunked steering, the task of maximizing a sequence-level reward with a chunked generator under a fixed number of denoiser evaluations, and propose LatticeSMC, a sampler derived from a Feynman-Kac model on the two-dimensional lattice of chunk index and denoising step. Two exact telescoping results make the design derivable: for chunk-additive rewards the two axes carry identical weights, so resampling belongs wherever lookahead is cheapest; for terminal rewards any prefix score yields an exact intermediate potential, so a prefix-evaluable reward is a twist with no estimation and no extra denoiser evaluations. LatticeSMC resamples properly on these exact potentials, at chunk boundaries and, when the plug-in reward is free, within chunks, and returns either a draw from its particle approximation of the reward-tilted target or its best particle, and recovers Feynman-Kac steering as its within-chunk schedule. Under matched compute, on a music-to-dance diffusion model and a 40-second text-to-music model, it raises beat alignment from 0.234 to 0.441 (best-of-N: 0.354) and prompt adherence from 0.470 to 0.560 at 32 particles with held-out quality metrics at base, holds its lead on the long-range reward at six and eight chunks, and is preferred by human raters over every comparator in 60 to 77 percent of pairwise judgements. Two measurable properties of the reward settle what remains: how hard to commit at a boundary follows the information in its exact potential, which the effective-sample-size gate reads off and greedy pruning cannot, and whether content-axis lookahead pays follows the within-set predictability of future reward, measured before any particle is spent. The source code is available at LatticeSMC .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Generative models for long-form sequential data increasingly produce their output in chunks: dance diffusion conditions each five-second window on the last ( Tseng et al., 2023 ) , latent text-to-music models generate a window that inpainting extends past its edge ( Evans et al., 2024 ; Evans et al., 2025 ) , and streaming video models denoise frame blocks against a growing context ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Yin et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025 ) . Each chunk is generated by iterative denoising ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ) , so a sequence is the result of a process with two clocks, the denoising step within a chunk and the chunk index, and the rewards that matter are rarely local to a chunk: a choreography must follow the beat for its whole duration and a song must match its prompt over forty seconds rather than its first ten. Spending inference-time compute to raise such rewards without retraining the generator is our setting. Each existing steering tool acts on a single axis of this process. Best-of-N draws complete sequences and keeps the best ( Brown et al., 2024 ; Ma et al., 2025 ) , spending every evaluation before any evidence arrives. Feynman-Kac steering ( Singhal et al., 2025 ; Skreta et al., 2025 ) resamples across denoising steps on plug-in rewards of partially denoised states, and twisted sequential Monte Carlo replaces the plug-in by a learned or refined twist ( Wu et al., 2023a ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Kim et al., 2026 ) ; for a chunked generator either means resampling on estimates of the current chunk while the sequence-level reward is out of reach. Streaming video systems prune candidate chunks after each block by greedy top- M M selection ( Tu et al., 2026 ) . These methods have been compared under different return rules and at budgets that do not charge the decoder and reward evaluations lookahead requires, so where on the two-clock lattice to place resampling events has had no principled answer. Our starting point is that every one of these methods is a choice of potentials and resampling events on one object, a Feynman-Kac model ( Del Moral, 2004 ; Chopin and Papaspiliopoulos, 2020 ) on the lattice of chunk index k k and denoising step τ \tau (Figure 1 ): best-of-N at the terminal corner, Feynman-Kac steering along the denoising axis, chunk pruning along the chunk axis with degenerate resampling. Two properties follow by telescoping: for a reward that decomposes over chunks, the product of a chunk’s denoising-axis potentials equals its chunk-axis potential exactly, so the two axes define the same tilted target with the same per-chunk weights and differ only in where resampling occurs; for a terminal reward, any prefix scores whose final value is the reward define exact intermediate potentials, so a prefix-evaluable reward is a twist with no estimation. LatticeSMC is the sampler these results prescribe: exact chunk rewards or prefix-score increments as potentials, so its target is the reward-tilted distribution without a learned component; resampling gated by effective sample size ( Kong et al., 1994 ) at chunk boundaries; a within-chunk schedule switched on only when plug-in evaluation is free, since axis equivalence says those events change the resampling times and not the weights; and two return modes, a weighted draw for sampling and the best particle for search. We evaluate LatticeSMC under matched denoiser evaluations on four sequence-level rewards across two modalities: beat alignment and a long-range repetition reward for a music-to-dance diffusion model on AIST++ ( Li et al., 2021 ) , and prompt adherence ( Wu et al., 2023b ) and motif recurrence for a 40-second text-to-music flow model. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: • We introduce the lattice Feynman-Kac model, a unifying formulation under which existing inference-time methods correspond to different placements of potentials. We further derive two telescoping results: identical axis weights for chunk-additive rewards and exact prefix-score potentials for terminal rewards. • We propose LatticeSMC, a training-free sampler whose every design decision follows directly from the model, with no learned components. • We derive practical criteria for commitment and lookahead. Commitment at each boundary should follow the information carried by its exact potential, which explains when the sharpest per-boundary tilt succeeds and when an ESS gate is required to preserve the particle set. Lookahead pays in proportion to the within-set predictability of future reward, a quantity measurable before sampling, which prefix-evaluable scores realize and learned regressors do not. • With 32 particles, LatticeSMC matches or outperforms every compared method on every reward, raising beat alignment from 0.234 to 0.441 (best-of-N: 0.354; chunk pruning: 0.415) and prompt adherence from 0.470 to 0.560 while preserving held-out quality. It matches Feynman-Kac steering at a quarter of the decoder calls, retains its advantage on long-range rewards at six and eight chunks, holds its ranking from 4M to 38M parameters, and is preferred by human raters. sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Inference-Time Compute and Search. Inference-time compute improves language-model outputs through repeated sampling with verifiers ( Brown et al., 2024 ) , process-level verification ( Lightman et al., 2024 ) , tree search over partial solutions ( Yao et al., 2023 ) , and adaptive allocation between sampling and revision ( Snell et al., 2025 ) ; controlled decoding similarly scores partial sequences with learned values ( Mudgal et al., 2024 ) . For diffusion models, analogous methods search over noises or trajectories ( Ma et al., 2025 ) or perform reward-guided test-time alignment ( Kim et al., 2025 ) . These approaches operate on a single generation clock. We instead treat chunk index and denoising step as two clocks of one process and study where inference-time compute should be allocated across this lattice. Reward-Guided Diffusion Sampling. Existing approaches broadly modify the sampling kernel, fine-tune the generator, or reweight a sample population. Kernel-based guidance includes classifier guidance ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ) , classifier-free guidance ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) , diffusion posterior sampling ( Chung et al., 2023 ) , and loss-guided sampling ( Song et al., 2023 ) ; see Uehara et al. (2025) . Fine-tuning methods optimize diffusion models with reinforcement learning ( Black et al., 2024 ; Fan et al., 2023 ) , reward gradients ( Clark et al., 2024 ) , or preference optimization ( Wallace et al., 2024 ) , but require reward-specific training and can over-optimize learned rewards ( Gao et al., 2023 ) . Population-based methods instead retain the kernel and use SMC during denoising ( Trippe et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2023a ; Dou and Song, 2024 ; Cardoso et al., 2024 ) , Feynman–Kac steering or correction ( Singhal et al., 2025 ; Skreta et al., 2025 ) , and refined or amortized twists ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Kim et al., 2026 ) . LatticeSMC belongs to this family but introduces the chunk axis, showing when chunk- and denoising-axis formulations coincide, when prefix scores define exact twists, and where resampling should be placed at matched cost. Kernel modification is complementary to this placement problem. Sequential Monte Carlo. LatticeSMC builds on bootstrap filtering ( Gordon et al., 1993 ) , ESS-based adaptive resampling ( Kong et al., 1994 ; Liu and Chen, 1998 ) , and low-variance resampling ( Douc et al., 2005 ) . Auxiliary particle filters and SMC samplers generalize these constructions ( Pitt and Shephard, 1999 ; Del Moral et al., 2006 ) , while twisting toward expected future weight is classical ( Whiteley and Lee, 2014 ; Guarniero et al., 2017 ; Heng et al., 2020 ) . The broader Feynman–Kac view is developed in Del Moral (2004) ; Chopin and Papaspiliopoulos (2020) ; Naesseth et al. (2019) . SMC has also been used for language generation with programmable potentials ( Lew et al., 2023 ) , learned twists ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , structured constraints ( Loula et al., 2025 ) , and rollout-based values ( Puri et al., 2025 ) . Our analysis connects the usefulness of twisting to the within-set predictability of future reward and therefore applies beyond the specific generators studied here. Chunked and Streaming Generators. Long-form generation often proceeds block by block. In video, diffusion forcing ( Chen et al., 2024 ) , rolling diffusion ( Ruhe et al., 2024 ) , and causal autoregressive distillation ( Yin et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025 ) generate or refine successive windows; streaming test-time scaling further prunes candidate blocks by reward ( Tu et al., 2026 ) . Music models similarly extend sequences autoregressively ( Copet et al., 2023 ) or through latent-diffusion inpainting ( Evans et al., 2024 ; Evans et al., 2025 ) . In dance, generation has progressed from token-based models ( Siyao et al., 2022 ) to diffusion approaches ( Tseng et al., 2023 ; Alexanderson et al., 2023 ) , with long-form choreography assembled from chunks or primitives ( Li et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ) . These systems focus on how to generate long sequences; our question is instead where inference-time compute should be spent across the chunk and denoising axes.

sections.heading: 3.4 LatticeSMC
sections.text: LatticeSMC is the sequential Monte Carlo sampler for the chunk-axis Feynman-Kac model with the potentials of Propositions 1 and 2 (Figure 1 (a); pseudocode in Appendix A.3 ). Potentials. For a chunk-additive reward the potential at the end of chunk k k is exp ⁡ ( r k ​ ( x ( ≤ k ) ) / α ) \exp(r_{k}(x^{(\leq k)})/\alpha) ; for a terminal reward with a prefix-evaluable score it is the increment potential of Proposition 2 with the terminal correction. Resampling. At the end of every chunk k < K k<K the weights are multiplied by the potential and, if ESS < N / 2 \mathrm{ESS}<N/2 , the set is resampled systematically ( Doucet and Johansen, 2011 ) and the weights reset; the gate keeps the set intact through chunks whose potential carries no information, such as the opening chunks of a motif-recurrence reward. When the plug-in reward is free, potentials can also sit at a fixed subset of denoising steps inside each chunk, with the same weights by Proposition 1 and earlier resampling times: the dense schedule. Return modes. After the last chunk the sampler returns a particle drawn in proportion to its weight (sampling mode: a draw from the particle approximation of π α \pi_{\alpha} , consistent as N → ∞ N\to\infty ) or the highest-reward particle (search mode). The cost is N ​ K ​ S NKS denoiser evaluations (times the guidance multiplicity), K ​ N KN reward evaluations and, on a latent generator, K ​ N KN decoder calls. Every other method is the same loop with a different set of lattice points at which the potential is not one and a different resampling operator, which is how all comparisons below are placed at equal budget; since a denoising-axis potential on a latent generator costs a decoder and a reward pass per particle per event, we also report model calls and wall-clock.

sections.heading: 4.1 Setup
sections.text: Generators (Appendix C.1 ). The first testbed is a music-to-dance diffusion model on AIST++ ( Li et al., 2021 ) in the EDGE representation ( Tseng et al., 2023 ) , made chunked by conditioning each 150-frame chunk on the clean previous one with the root integrated from the prefix, so the prefix is fixed and the seam continuous; it generates K = 4 K=4 chunks of 5 s ( K = 6 K=6 and 8 8 in Section 4.4 ) with S = 50 S=50 DDIM steps ( Song et al., 2021 ) and classifier-free guidance, at 4M and 38M parameters. The second is a 40-second text-to-music flow model ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) that extends a clip by inpainting past its edge with the prefix latents replaced at each of its S = 8 S=8 steps, K = 4 K=4 chunks of 10 s; each prefix score costs one decode and one CLAP ( Wu et al., 2023b ) pass, which we count. Rewards. On dance, beat alignment is chunk-additive and chunk-local (kinematic beats against music beats), and repetition scores chunk k k against chunk k − 2 k-2 , additive but long range, with no signal until the third chunk; it is a controlled long-range reward, not a quality target (real dancers score 0.412 0.412 , the base model 0.718 0.718 ). On music, prompt adherence is the CLAP score of the full clip against its prompt, terminal and evaluable on any prefix, and motif recurrence the similarity of the last chunk to the first, with a prefix score at the last boundary. Held out from every steering decision are physical plausibility, realism and pose diversity on dance, and tempo adherence, spectral energy, aesthetics ( Tjandra et al., 2025 ) , seam continuity and embedding diversity on music (Appendix C.2 ). Methods and Budget. All methods run in the same loop with the same kernels and noise streams: best-of-N with importance draw and with argmax, chunk pruning in the manner of Stream-T1 ( Tu et al., 2026 ) , its top- k k retention isolated at M = max ⁡ ( 1 , N / 4 ) M=\max(1,N/4) over the common kernel (swept in Section 4.4 ), learned-twist SMC on dance (Section 5 ), and LatticeSMC with the chunk potential on the dance rewards and the prefix-score potential on the music rewards, its dense schedule scoring at five (dance) or four (music) steps per chunk. We run LatticeSMC with both schedules. Its dense schedule is the Feynman-Kac steering placement: on a chunk-additive reward the two are the same algorithm (Proposition 1 ), and on the music rewards the plug-in CLAP differences telescope to the prefix-score increments of Proposition 2 (products agreeing to 10 − 14 10^{-14} on every stored lineage), so that row is the strongest form of the baseline and our own schedule at once. The temperature is set from base samples before any steered sample exists (Appendix A.5 ): α = 0.0068 \alpha=0.0068 and 0.019 0.019 on the two music rewards, and the sharpest value of the sweep α ∈ { 0.2 , 0.05 , 0.02 } \alpha\in\{0.2,0.05,0.02\} on dance, reported in full (Table 12 ) and shared by every method. sections.heading: 4.2 Chunk-axis resampling is the compute-efficient placement
sections.text: Figure 2 plots reward against denoiser evaluations, Table 1 the N = 32 N=32 endpoint under both return rules, and Tables 12 to 15 every budget. Three results hold across every reward, modality and model size. First, selecting at chunk boundaries beats selecting at the end: under the draw rule the chunk potentials raise the reward over terminal importance sampling by 0.038 0.038 on beat alignment, 0.028 0.028 on repetition and 0.020 0.020 on prompt adherence at N = 32 N=32 (intervals exclude zero), and under the search rule the gaps are larger: with its prescribed schedule LatticeSMC reaches 0.441 0.441 on beat alignment against 0.354 0.354 for best-of-N argmax, 0.962 0.962 against 0.901 0.901 on repetition, 0.560 0.560 against 0.530 0.530 on prompt adherence and 0.929 0.929 against 0.918 0.918 on motif recurrence. On dance that schedule is the Feynman-Kac steering placement; the lattice view adds the exactness proof, the matched-compute comparison under one return rule, and the boundary schedule, which matches it under the sampling rule at a fifth of the reward evaluations. Second, under a common return rule, ESS-gated resampling beats top- M M replication at M = N / 4 M=N/4 at the largest budgets on every reward, and at every M M on the long-range rewards (Section 4.4 ). sections.heading: 4.5 Human evaluation
sections.text: To test whether a higher reward is perceptible and costs no quality that metrics miss, we ran a pairwise preference study on the two rewards with a direct perceptual reading, beat alignment and prompt adherence (Appendix D ). For each of the 40 conditions of each testbed, five Prolific raters compared the sequence returned by LatticeSMC (prescribed schedule, argmax, N = 32 N=32 ) against the base model, best-of-N argmax and chunk pruning, with side and order randomized and attention checks, on two questions: which follows the beat or matches the description better, and which they would rather watch or hear (Table 17 ). On the reward question LatticeSMC is preferred over the base model in 73.5 percent of dance and 77.0 percent of music judgements, over best-of-N in 66.0 and 69.0, and over chunk pruning in 69.0 and 71.5; on the overall question its win rate against every comparator is 60.5 to 69.0 percent; all twelve intervals lie above 50 percent. Per-condition reward differences and win rates correlate positively for every comparator (Spearman ρ \rho 0.23 0.23 to 0.67 0.67 ): the reward gain is perceptible and does not cost perceived quality.

sections.heading: 5.2 A design rule
sections.text: A twist has three sources (Figure 3 (c), Appendix B ): a prefix-evaluable reward, exact by Proposition 2 at no extra denoiser cost ( + 0.020 +0.020 terminal CLAP at N = 32 N=32 ); rollouts, unbiased but charged, which set the headroom ( + 0.058 +0.058 on repetition) yet lose to additional particles at matched cost for M ≤ 4 M\leq 4 ; and a learned predictor, whose rollout-derived targets carry about 2 nats of Monte Carlo error against a within-set spread of about 3, so that none we trained recovered a within-set ranking. Resample on the exact potentials with ESS gating, so that commitment follows the information each boundary carries, and set the tilt by the objective: under search, as sharp as the reward’s arrival allows, up to the α → 0 \alpha\to 0 corner for a chunk-local reward; under sampling, α \alpha defines the target; in both, hold it fixed per boundary across horizons. Then measure ρ k \rho_{k} from base-model rollouts before adding lookahead: if it is small, add none; if the reward can be evaluated on a prefix, use the prefix score at full strength; if not, validate any estimated twist by its within-set correlation and residual in nats, never by its cross-prompt fit.

sections.heading: 6 DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
sections.text: Inference-time steering of a chunked generator is one Feynman-Kac model on the lattice of chunk index and denoising step, and two telescoping identities fix its target: identical axis weights for chunk-additive rewards, and exact prefix-score twists for terminal rewards. LatticeSMC, the sampler they prescribe, ties or leads every method of the main comparison at matched compute across four rewards, two model sizes, and three horizons, while human evaluators also prefer its outputs. The remaining design choices are largely determined by two properties of the reward. First, commit at each boundary in proportion to the information carried by its exact potential, which ESS gating can read off adaptively and greedy pruning cannot. Second, add lookahead only in proportion to the within-set predictability of the future reward, so that extra compute is spent only when future scores are sufficiently informative for the current candidate set. Limitations. The horizon study is on dance, since the music generator’s 40 s context does not carry the prompted tempo over 80 s (Appendix C.6 ); the dance generators are small models trained for this study; the human study covers two rewards; gradient guidance, which composes with every placement, is not compared; and the propositions fix the target, not finite-particle behaviour, so a bound relating ρ k \rho_{k} to the incremental-weight variance is open.

sections.heading: A.2 The plug-in potential and the optimal twist
sections.text: Along the denoising axis, for a chunk-additive reward, the optimal twist at step τ \tau of chunk k k for the current chunk’s term is ψ k , τ ​ ( s k , τ ) = 𝔼 p ​ [ exp ⁡ ( r k / α ) ∣ s k , τ ] \psi_{k,\tau}(s_{k,\tau})=\mathbb{E}_{p}\big[\exp(r_{k}/\alpha)\mid s_{k,\tau}\big] . Feynman-Kac steering replaces it by the plug-in exp ⁡ ( r ^ k , τ / α ) \exp\big(\hat{r}_{k,\tau}/\alpha\big) with r ^ \hat{r} evaluated on the posterior-mean prediction x ^ 0 \hat{x}_{0} . Since u ↦ exp ⁡ ( u / α ) u\mapsto\exp(u/\alpha) is convex, Jensen’s inequality gives ψ k , τ ≥ exp ⁡ ( 𝔼 ⁡ [ r k ∣ s k , τ ] / α ) \psi_{k,\tau}\geq\exp\big(\mathbb{E}[r_{k}\mid s_{k,\tau}]/\alpha\big) , and the plug-in approximates the right-hand side up to the further gap between r k ​ ( x ^ 0 ) r_{k}(\hat{x}_{0}) and 𝔼 ⁡ [ r k ∣ s k , τ ] \mathbb{E}[r_{k}\mid s_{k,\tau}] for a nonlinear reward. Both gaps grow with the conditional variance of the current chunk given the noisy state, which is largest at the early denoising steps and vanishes at τ = S \tau=S , where the prediction is the sample. This is the sense in which denoising-axis lookahead on the current chunk is accurate late and uninformative early; Proposition 1 guarantees that whatever the plug-in’s accuracy at intermediate steps, the chunk’s weight at its end is exact, which fixes the target and not the finite-particle behaviour of the intermediate resampling events.

sections.heading: A.5 Implementation details
sections.text: Noise Streams and Reproducibility. Each particle slot i i of chunk k k draws its denoising noise from a generator seeded by ( seed , k , i ) (\text{seed},k,i) , and a resampled particle continues with the stream of the slot it occupies. Every resampling decision and the final draw consume a separate generator seeded by ( seed , method ) (\text{seed},\text{method}) . Two runs of any method with the same seed produce bitwise-identical particle systems, and a method whose potentials are all one reproduces the base sampler bitwise, which is the check we use to validate every implementation. Effective Sample Size and Resampling. With normalized weights w ¯ i = w i / ∑ j w j \bar{w}_{i}=w_{i}/\sum_{j}w_{j} , ESS = 1 / ∑ i w ¯ i 2 \mathrm{ESS}=1/\sum_{i}\bar{w}_{i}^{2} . Systematic resampling draws a single uniform u ∼ 𝒰 [ 0 , 1 / N ) u\sim\mathcal{U}[0,1/N) and selects the particles whose cumulative weight intervals contain u + j / N u+j/N for j = 0 , … , N − 1 j=0,\dots,N-1 ; it preserves the expected count of every particle and, in practice though not in general, has lower variance than multinomial resampling ( Douc et al., 2005 ) . Cost Accounting. The denoiser-evaluation counter is incremented by the number of rows in every denoiser forward call, so classifier-free guidance implemented as a doubled batch is charged twice per particle per step and guidance implemented as a single conditioned pass is charged once, matching the generator’s actual cost. Decoder calls and reward evaluations are separate counters. For every reported sequence the counters are audited against the closed-form value N ​ K ​ S NKS times the guidance multiplicity. Hardware, Software and Timing. All runs used two NVIDIA RTX A6000 (48 GB) GPUs in one machine. The dance harness runs PyTorch 2.14 (CUDA 13.0) in float32 with TF32 off, deterministic algorithms and cuDNN determinism on, the math attention kernel only, and all noise drawn from CPU generators; the music harness runs PyTorch 2.7.1 (CUDA 12.6) in the checkpoint’s parameter precisions with a decoder seed pinned per (prompt, seed). Bitwise reproduction was verified by regenerating the 160 base sequences of each dance model three times, once with every sequence moved to the other physical GPU (maximum absolute difference 0), by the argmax regenerations, which reproduce the stored particle sets in 160 of 160 dance and 320 of 320 music replays, and by the music latents and waveforms across processes; a chunk generated inside a batch of N N particles differs from the same chunk generated alone by up to 6 × 10 − 5 6\times 10^{-5} , so reproduction holds for a fixed (method, N N ). Wall-clock per sequence is the generating process’s own timer, averaged over the 80 sequences of the N = 32 N=32 row, with three processes per GPU sharing the two GPUs and the N N particles of a sequence forming one denoiser batch, in a single run; sharing inflates the absolute values, and the ratios between methods run under the same sharing are the quantity used. Numerical Verification of the Propositions. On every steered sequence, the sum of log-potentials along the returned particle’s lineage is compared with r ⁡ ( x ) / α r(x)/\alpha ; the maximum absolute discrepancy over all sequences, methods and schedules is below 10 − 13 10^{-13} in double precision. The identity of Proposition 2 at β = 0 \beta=0 is checked in its discrete form: the sampler with β = 0 \beta=0 reproduces best-of-N importance sampling bitwise, including the final draw. Temperature. On music the temperature is set from base samples before any steered sequence exists, by the rule α = Δ / ln ⁡ 10 3 \alpha=\Delta/\ln 10^{3} , where Δ \Delta is the mean over conditions of the interdecile range of the reward over that condition’s base samples and their continuations; this makes the maximum weight ratio across a particle set of order 10 3 10^{3} at the terminal corner and is the same for every method. On dance the sweep α ∈ { 0.2 , 0.05 , 0.02 } \alpha\in\{0.2,0.05,0.02\} is reported in full (Table 12 ); the implied maximum weight ratio across 32 particles at these values is 3 3 , about 80 80 and about 10 4 10^{4} .

sections.heading: Appendix B Lookahead: Measurements and Twist Details
sections.text: A twist has three sources (Figure 3 (c)). A prefix-evaluable reward is an exact intermediate potential by Proposition 2 , with no estimation and no extra denoiser evaluations; it raises terminal CLAP by 0.020 0.020 at N = 32 N=32 over terminal importance sampling, monotonically in β \beta . Rollouts, M M continuations per particle averaging exp ⁡ ( S k / α ) \exp(S_{k}/\alpha) , are an unbiased twist that establishes the headroom, + 0.058 +0.058 at N = 32 N=32 with sixteen continuations on repetition, but charged at their cost they lose to additional particles for M ≤ 4 M\leq 4 (Appendix B.4 ). A learned predictor is the cheapest twist, but its rollout-derived targets carry a Monte Carlo error of about 2 nats against a within-set spread of about 3, so they hold no within-set ranking to learn; one trained directly on within-set weights reaches a within-set correlation of 0.08 0.08 to 0.13 0.13 (Appendix B.3 ).

sections.heading: B.2 Within-set accuracy of a twist
sections.text: For a particle set produced by the sampler at chunk k k , the oracle twist log ⁡ ψ k ⋆ \log\psi^{\star}_{k} of every particle is computed from M = 16 M=16 continuations to the end. A candidate twist’s within-set accuracy is the Pearson (and Spearman) correlation between its log ⁡ ψ k \log\psi_{k} and log ⁡ ψ k ⋆ \log\psi^{\star}_{k} across the N N particles of the set, averaged over sets; its weight-level error is the standard deviation of log ⁡ ψ k − log ⁡ ψ k ⋆ \log\psi_{k}-\log\psi^{\star}_{k} within a set after removing the set mean, since the set mean cancels in the normalized weights. The primary learned twist is a multilayer perceptron ( 4,638 → 512 → 512 → 1 4{,}638\to 512\to 512\to 1 , ReLU, inputs standardized) whose input is the last 30 frames of the prefix in the chunk’s own root frame, the mean-pooled music features of each remaining chunk and a one-hot chunk index; it is trained on 4,000 prefixes (3,500 training, 500 validation) with rollout targets log ⁡ 1 M ​ ∑ m exp ⁡ ( S p , m / α ) \log\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m}\exp(S_{p,m}/\alpha) at M = 8 M=8 (Monte Carlo standard error about 0.5 0.5 nats), by mean-squared error with Adam (learning rate 10 − 3 10^{-3} , weight decay 10 − 4 10^{-4} , batch 256, 300 epochs, the checkpoint with the lowest validation error kept), and evaluated on 500 fresh prefixes with fresh rollouts. Its residual column in Table 4 is the root-mean-square error against those targets across prefixes; within a set, after removing the set mean, the residual standard deviation is 6.0 6.0 nats. Its residual on held-out prefixes decomposes into a between-sequence component (0.27 of its variance) and a within-sequence component (0.73), so most of its error is of the kind that does not cancel.

The effect on the returned reward at N = 32 N=32 moves from − 0.053 -0.053 to − 0.017 -0.017 , + 0.003 +0.003 and − 0.002 -0.002 , the last two indistinguishable from ψ ≡ 1 \psi\equiv 1 , and the fraction of early boundaries at which the sampler resamples falls from 1.00 1.00 to 0.05 0.05 . sections.heading: B.5 Denoising-axis plug-in accuracy
sections.text: Along the denoising axis the plug-in prediction of the current chunk’s own reward is evaluated against the realized reward of the same continuation at DDIM steps 45, 35, 25, 15 and 5 of 50 on 500 fresh prefixes. For the repetition reward its R 2 R^{2} is 0.995 0.995 , 0.985 0.985 , 0.974 0.974 , 0.952 0.952 and 0.858 0.858 ; for beat alignment the plug-in explains 0.40 0.40 of the variance at step 45 and none from step 35 on, its correlation with the realized reward falling to 0.11 0.11 at step 5. This is the Jensen-gap ordering of Appendix A.2 : chunk-local lookahead is accurate late in denoising and exact at the chunk’s end, so within-chunk resampling events leave the chunk weight exact when the plug-in is free to score; what they change is the resampling times, whose finite-particle effect Section 4.2 measures.

sections.heading: C.1 Testbeds
sections.text: Figure 4: Two chunked generators. Top: music-to-dance diffusion on AIST++. The denoiser sees a 300-frame window, the clean prefix chunk and the noisy chunk, and predicts the chunk’s root as a displacement integrated from the prefix root, so the prefix is fixed and the seam continuous by construction; steering rewards are beat alignment (chunk-additive) and repetition of chunk k k against chunk k − 2 k-2 (long range). Bottom: text-to-music flow, 40 s as four 10 s chunks. Each chunk is generated by inpainting past the clip’s edge with the prefix latents replaced at every flow step; scoring a prefix requires one decode and one CLAP pass, which is charged; steering rewards are prompt adherence (terminal, evaluable on any prefix) and motif recurrence of the last chunk against the first. Chunked Dance Diffusion. The base model is a transformer denoiser in the EDGE representation ( Tseng et al., 2023 ) (151 channels: foot contacts, root translation and 6D joint rotations at 30 fps) trained on AIST++ ( Li et al., 2021 ) with EDGE’s per-frame losses. Chunking is obtained by training on pairs of consecutive 150-frame windows: the input is a 300-frame window whose first half is the clean prefix chunk and whose second half is the noised chunk, with a binary prefix-indicator channel, and the loss is computed on the second half, with the velocity and foot-sliding terms at the seam evaluated against the clean prefix frame. With probability 0.2 0.2 the prefix is replaced by zeros to train the unconditional start of a sequence. The generated chunk predicts its root as a per-frame displacement in metres, normalized by its training standard deviation and integrated from the prefix root at sampling time, so root continuity at the seam holds by construction; the pose seam is checked by the ratio of the joint-position jump at the seam to the median within-chunk jump, 2.87 2.87 for the 4M model and 2.27 2.27 for the 38M model against 0.93 0.93 for ground truth. The 4M model (latent 192, feed-forward 384, 4 layers, 4 heads, dropout 0.1, 4.06M parameters) is scheduled for 18,000 steps and the 38M model (latent 512, feed-forward 1024, 6 layers, 8 heads, 37.6M parameters) for 36,000, at batch 64 with Adan (learning rate 4 × 10 − 4 4\times 10^{-4} , weight decay 0.02, constant schedule), EDGE’s cosine schedule with 1,000 diffusion steps and x 0 x_{0} prediction, condition dropout 0.25, and EDGE’s loss weights (simple 0.636, velocity 2.964, forward-kinematic 0.646, foot contact 10.942) applied to the chunk half of the window; the audio features are EDGE’s 35-dimensional baseline features at 30 fps, whose beat channel the reward reads. Training uses 7,090 windows of 300 frames from the training sequences and 2,620 from held-out sequences for monitoring; each model adopts the checkpoint with the lowest held-out loss (step 12,000 and step 9,000). The full configuration files are in the supplementary material. Sampling is EDGE’s DDIM schedule with 50 steps, η = 1 \eta=1 and guidance weight 2, so a chunk costs 2 × 50 2\times 50 denoiser rows per particle. Ninety-six music-and-motion sequences are held out at the sequence level; prompts are 20-second music segments from held-out sequences, two per music piece across all ten genres, 40 in total, with four seeds each. Chunked Text-to-Music Flow. The base model is Stable Audio 3 Medium ( Stability AI, 2026 ) , a 44.1 kHz stereo latent flow-matching transformer ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) with an autoencoder (Hugging Face stabilityai/stable-audio-3-medium , revision 27b5a21 ), run at its shipped settings (8 ping-pong steps, guidance 1.0, so one denoiser row per particle per step; denoiser in bf16, decoder in fp16 as shipped); the decoder is the checkpoint’s own autoencoder, and the CLAP scorer is the LAION HTSAT-base music checkpoint music_audioset_epoch_15_esc_90.14 ( Wu et al., 2023b ) . The chunked extension is this study’s adaptation of inpainting-based extension: each new 10-second chunk is generated with the previous latents present, and at every flow step the latent region of the prefix is overwritten with the fixed prefix latents noised to that step, so the particle state is bit-exact across chunks. The decoder is stochastic and is given a seed fixed per (prompt, seed) pair, which makes waveforms reproducible across processes. The seam spectral-flux ratio of the raw decode is 1.26 1.26 (a within-chunk control gives 1.21 1.21 ), tempo adherence of base samples to the prompted tempo is 0.95 0.95 within 5 percent, and CLAP prompt retrieval over 10 genre-diverse prompts is 0.65 0.65 at rank 1 (chance 0.1 0.1 ). Prompts are 40 templated descriptions (8 genres, instrumentation, an explicit tempo, no structural words), with two seeds each.

sections.heading: C.2 Rewards and held-out metrics
sections.text: Beat Alignment. Kinematic beats are local minima of the smoothed mean joint speed of the generated motion ( Siyao et al., 2022 ) ; the reward is the mean over music beats of exp ( − d 2 / 2 σ 2 ) \exp(-d^{2}/2\sigma^{2}) with d d the distance in frames to the nearest kinematic beat and σ = 3 \sigma=3 frames. Its chunk-additive form assigns each music beat to its chunk and evaluates it against the kinematic beats of the prefix through that chunk; the mean absolute gap between the additive and full forms is 0.01 0.01 on every method. Repetition. r k = exp ( − d k / τ ) r_{k}=\exp(-d_{k}/\tau) for k ≥ 3 k\geq 3 with d k d_{k} the mean root-relative joint-position distance between chunk k k and chunk k − 2 k-2 and τ = 0.171 \tau=0.171 m, the median of d d over base samples; r 1 = r 2 = 0 r_{1}=r_{2}=0 . The additive and full forms coincide exactly. Real dancers score 0.412 0.412 on this reward and the base model 0.718 0.718 . Prompt Adherence. The cosine similarity between the CLAP audio embedding of the clip and the CLAP text embedding of its prompt, with the LAION music checkpoint ( Wu et al., 2023b ) ; a 40-second clip is embedded as the renormalized mean of its four 10-second window embeddings. The prefix score s k s_{k} is the same quantity on the decoded prefix through chunk k k ; the additive counterpart, the mean of the window scores, differs from the terminal value by under 2 percent. Motif Recurrence. The cosine similarity between the CLAP audio embeddings of the fourth and first 10-second windows of the returned clip; the prefix score is the similarity of the third window to the first, available at the last boundary. On base samples 99.4 99.4 percent of clips have a final window closer to their own opening than to another prompt’s, so the reward moves within the model’s own notion of a returning motif. Held-out Metrics. On dance: EDGE’s physical foot-contact score (PFC), a realism statistic (the 1-Wasserstein distance between the per-frame joint-acceleration distribution of a sample and that of held-out real motion), root travel per sequence, and pose diversity (mean pairwise root-relative joint distance across the seeds of a condition). On music: tempo adherence (fraction of chunks whose tracked tempo is within 5 percent of the prompted tempo, with a neural beat tracker ( Foscarin et al., 2024 ) ), the fraction of energy above 8 kHz, the four audiobox-aesthetics axes ( Tjandra et al., 2025 ) , the seam spectral-flux ratio, and embedding diversity (mean pairwise CLAP cosine distance across seeds). None is used by any method.

sections.heading: C.3 Cost accounting and compute
sections.text: Denoiser rows, decoder calls and reward evaluations are counted per sequence and audited against their closed forms; per sequence at N = 32 N=32 the music methods make 32 (best-of-N), 128 (pruning and LatticeSMC on prompt adherence, where every boundary is scored; 64 on motif recurrence, whose prefix score exists only at the last boundary) and 512 (dense schedule on prompt adherence) decoder and CLAP calls. Wall-clock is measured with three processes sharing a GPU, so the ratios between methods are the informative quantity. The main study, including the scale replicate and the lookahead measurements of Appendix B , used about 250 GPU-hours on two 48 GB GPUs; the pruning sweep, the horizon and temperature runs and the music qualification of Appendices C.5 and C.6 used about 110 more, measured as summed job walls on GPUs shared with other jobs.

For each of the 40 conditions of each testbed and generation seed 2000, the sequence returned by LatticeSMC (prescribed schedule, argmax, N = 32 N=32 , α \alpha as in Section 4.1 ) was paired with the sequence returned by the base model, by best-of-N argmax and by chunk pruning ( M = N / 4 M=N/4 ) at the same budget, giving 40 pairs per comparator, 120 pairs per testbed and 240 pairs in total. Dance sequences were rendered as SMPL ( Loper et al., 2015 ) mesh videos at 30 fps with a fixed camera and the conditioning music as the soundtrack; music clips were the 40-second decodes, loudness-normalized to − 14 -14 LUFS. Within a pair both sequences share the condition and the seed, so raters heard the same music for both dances or read the same description for both clips, and method identities were hidden throughout. Raters. Participants were recruited on Prolific and were required to be fluent in English, to have an approval rate of at least 95 percent and at least 100 completed studies, and to pass a headphone screening check. Each participant judged 20 substantive pairs from one testbed in a session of about 40 minutes and received US$12, a target rate of US$18 per hour. Two instructed-response attention checks were interleaved with the substantive pairs, and participants failing both were excluded: 4 of 64, leaving 60 retained participants, 30 per testbed, with replacement sessions restoring five valid ratings per pair. The retained data comprise 1,200 pair evaluations and 2,400 answers across the two questions. Pair order and the side assigned to LatticeSMC were randomized independently per participant. Questions. For each pair raters answered, in order: (1) Which dance follows the beat of the music better? for dance, or Which clip better matches the description shown? for music; (2) Which would you rather watch? for dance, or Which would you rather listen to? for music. Each question offered A, B and no preference. Question (1) reads the dimension the steering reward targets; question (2) reads overall preference. Statistics. Existing inference-time steering methods act on one axis of this process at a time, best-of-N at the end, Feynman-Kac steering across denoising steps, streaming pipelines across chunks, and have been compared under different return rules at unmatched compute. We introduce budget-matched chunked steering, the task of maximizing a sequence-level reward with a chunked generator under a fixed number of denoiser evaluations, and propose LatticeSMC, a sampler derived from a Feynman-Kac model on the two-dimensional lattice of chunk index and denoising step. Two exact telescoping results make the design derivable: for chunk-additive rewards the two axes carry identical weights, so resampling belongs wherever lookahead is cheapest; for terminal rewards any prefix score yields an exact intermediate potential, so a prefix-evaluable reward is a twist with no estimation and no extra denoiser evaluations. LatticeSMC resamples properly on these exact potentials, at chunk boundaries and, when the plug-in reward is free, within chunks, and returns either a draw from its particle approximation of the reward-tilted target or its best particle, and recovers Feynman-Kac steering as its within-chunk schedule. Under matched compute, on a music-to-dance diffusion model and a 40-second text-to-music model, it raises beat alignment from 0.234 to 0.441 (best-of-N: 0.354) and prompt adherence from 0.470 to 0.560 at 32 particles with held-out quality metrics at base, holds its lead on the long-range reward at six and eight chunks, and is preferred by human raters over every comparator in 60 to 77 percent of pairwise judgements. Two measurable properties of the reward settle what remains: how hard to commit at a boundary follows the information in its exact potential, which the effective-sample-size gate reads off and greedy pruning cannot, and whether content-axis lookahead pays follows the within-set predictability of future reward, measured before any particle is spent. The source code is available at LatticeSMC . 1 Introduction Generative models for long-form sequential data increasingly produce their output in chunks: dance diffusion conditions each five-second window on the last ( Tseng et al., 2023 ) , latent text-to-music models generate a window that inpainting extends past its edge ( Evans et al., 2024 ; Evans et al., 2025 ) , and streaming video models denoise frame blocks against a growing context ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Yin et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025 ) . Each chunk is generated by iterative denoising ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ) , so a sequence is the result of a process with two clocks, the denoising step within a chunk and the chunk index, and the rewards that matter are rarely local to a chunk: a choreography must follow the beat for its whole duration and a song must match its prompt over forty seconds rather than its first ten. Spending inference-time compute to raise such rewards without retraining the generator is our setting. Each existing steering tool acts on a single axis of this process. Best-of-N draws complete sequences and keeps the best ( Brown et al., 2024 ; Ma et al., 2025 ) , spending every evaluation before any evidence arrives. Feynman-Kac steering ( Singhal et al., 2025 ; Skreta et al., 2025 ) resamples across denoising steps on plug-in rewards of partially denoised states, and twisted sequential Monte Carlo replaces the plug-in by a learned or refined twist ( Wu et al., 2023a ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Kim et al., 2026 ) ; for a chunked generator either means resampling on estimates of the current chunk while the sequence-level reward is out of reach. Streaming video systems prune candidate chunks after each block by greedy top- M M selection ( Tu et al., 2026 ) . These methods have been compared under different return rules and at budgets that do not charge the decoder and reward evaluations lookahead requires, so where on the two-clock lattice to place resampling events has had no principled answer. Our starting point is that every one of these methods is a choice of potentials and resampling events on one object, a Feynman-Kac model ( Del Moral, 2004 ; Chopin and Papaspiliopoulos, 2020 ) on the lattice of chunk index k k and denoising step τ \tau (Figure 1 ): best-of-N at the terminal corner, Feynman-Kac steering along the denoising axis, chunk pruning along the chunk axis with degenerate resampling. Two properties follow by telescoping: for a reward that decomposes over chunks, the product of a chunk’s denoising-axis potentials equals its chunk-axis potential exactly, so the two axes define the same tilted target with the same per-chunk weights and differ only in where resampling occurs; for a terminal reward, any prefix scores whose final value is the reward define exact intermediate potentials, so a prefix-evaluable reward is a twist with no estimation. LatticeSMC is the sampler these results prescribe: exact chunk rewards or prefix-score increments as potentials, so its target is the reward-tilted distribution without a learned component; resampling gated by effective sample size ( Kong et al., 1994 ) at chunk boundaries; a within-chunk schedule switched on only when plug-in evaluation is free, since axis equivalence says those events change the resampling times and not the weights; and two return modes, a weighted draw for sampling and the best particle for search. We evaluate LatticeSMC under matched denoiser evaluations on four sequence-level rewards across two modalities: beat alignment and a long-range repetition reward for a music-to-dance diffusion model on AIST++ ( Li et al., 2021 ) , and prompt adherence ( Wu et al., 2023b ) and motif recurrence for a 40-second text-to-music flow model. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: • We introduce the lattice Feynman-Kac model, a unifying formulation under which existing inference-time methods correspond to different placements of potentials. We further derive two telescoping results: identical axis weights for chunk-additive rewards and exact prefix-score potentials for terminal rewards. • We propose LatticeSMC, a training-free sampler whose every design decision follows directly from the model, with no learned components. • We derive practical criteria for commitment and lookahead. Commitment at each boundary should follow the information carried by its exact potential, which explains when the sharpest per-boundary tilt succeeds and when an ESS gate is required to preserve the particle set. Lookahead pays in proportion to the within-set predictability of future reward, a quantity measurable before sampling, which prefix-evaluable scores realize and learned regressors do not. • With 32 particles, LatticeSMC matches or outperforms every compared method on every reward, raising beat alignment from 0.234 to 0.441 (best-of-N: 0.354; chunk pruning: 0.415) and prompt adherence from 0.470 to 0.560 while preserving held-out quality. It matches Feynman-Kac steering at a quarter of the decoder calls, retains its advantage on long-range rewards at six and eight chunks, holds its ranking from 4M to 38M parameters, and is preferred by human raters. Inference-time compute improves language-model outputs through repeated sampling with verifiers ( Brown et al., 2024 ) , process-level verification ( Lightman et al., 2024 ) , tree search over partial solutions ( Yao et al., 2023 ) , and adaptive allocation between sampling and revision ( Snell et al., 2025 ) ; controlled decoding similarly scores partial sequences with learned values ( Mudgal et al., 2024 ) . For diffusion models, analogous methods search over noises or trajectories ( Ma et al., 2025 ) or perform reward-guided test-time alignment ( Kim et al., 2025 ) . These approaches operate on a single generation clock. We instead treat chunk index and denoising step as two clocks of one process and study where inference-time compute should be allocated across this lattice. Reward-Guided Diffusion Sampling. Existing approaches broadly modify the sampling kernel, fine-tune the generator, or reweight a sample population. Kernel-based guidance includes classifier guidance ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ) , classifier-free guidance ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) , diffusion posterior sampling ( Chung et al., 2023 ) , and loss-guided sampling ( Song et al., 2023 ) ; see Uehara et al. (2025) . Fine-tuning methods optimize diffusion models with reinforcement learning ( Black et al., 2024 ; Fan et al., 2023 ) , reward gradients ( Clark et al., 2024 ) , or preference optimization ( Wallace et al., 2024 ) , but require reward-specific training and can over-optimize learned rewards ( Gao et al., 2023 ) . Population-based methods instead retain the kernel and use SMC during denoising ( Trippe et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2023a ; Dou and Song, 2024 ; Cardoso et al., 2024 ) , Feynman–Kac steering or correction ( Singhal et al., 2025 ; Skreta et al., 2025 ) , and refined or amortized twists ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Kim et al., 2026 ) . LatticeSMC belongs to this family but introduces the chunk axis, showing when chunk- and denoising-axis formulations coincide, when prefix scores define exact twists, and where resampling should be placed at matched cost. Kernel modification is complementary to this placement problem. Sequential Monte Carlo. LatticeSMC builds on bootstrap filtering ( Gordon et al., 1993 ) , ESS-based adaptive resampling ( Kong et al., 1994 ; Liu and Chen, 1998 ) , and low-variance resampling ( Douc et al., 2005 ) . Auxiliary particle filters and SMC samplers generalize these constructions ( Pitt and Shephard, 1999 ; Del Moral et al., 2006 ) , while twisting toward expected future weight is classical ( Whiteley and Lee, 2014 ; Guarniero et al., 2017 ; Heng et al., 2020 ) . The broader Feynman–Kac view is developed in Del Moral (2004) ; Chopin and Papaspiliopoulos (2020) ; Naesseth et al. (2019) . SMC has also been used for language generation with programmable potentials ( Lew et al., 2023 ) , learned twists ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , structured constraints ( Loula et al., 2025 ) , and rollout-based values ( Puri et al., 2025 ) . Our analysis connects the usefulness of twisting to the within-set predictability of future reward and therefore applies beyond the specific generators studied here. Chunked and Streaming Generators. Long-form generation often proceeds block by block. In video, diffusion forcing ( Chen et al., 2024 ) , rolling diffusion ( Ruhe et al., 2024 ) , and causal autoregressive distillation ( Yin et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025 ) generate or refine successive windows; streaming test-time scaling further prunes candidate blocks by reward ( Tu et al., 2026 ) . Music models similarly extend sequences autoregressively ( Copet et al., 2023 ) or through latent-diffusion inpainting ( Evans et al., 2024 ; Evans et al., 2025 ) . In dance, generation has progressed from token-based models ( Siyao et al., 2022 ) to diffusion approaches ( Tseng et al., 2023 ; Alexanderson et al., 2023 ) , with long-form choreography assembled from chunks or primitives ( Li et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ) .
